paragraphs.text: When the national museums of one European country abolished entry charges in 2001, visitor numbers rose by an average of 70 per cent within five years. The increase was largest at museums outside the capital.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The change was not free for taxpayers. The government paid the museums an extra grant to replace lost ticket income, although officials argued that the cost was balanced by more spending in museum shops and cafés.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Critics noted that most of the new visitors came from groups who already visited museums often. People from low-income areas, whom the policy was partly meant to attract, increased their visits only slightly.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Some museums have since introduced charges for special exhibitions while keeping the permanent collections free. Their directors say this has raised money without reducing overall visitor numbers.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Several other countries have since studied the policy, but few have copied it in full, mainly because of the cost to national budgets.
paragraphs.label: E
